page.title: Fluency substitution
page.description: A teaching figure: two students hand in the same AI-drafted paper, and only changing one fact shows which of them owns the call.
page.setup: {A_person} asks an AI to draft a strategy recommendation, reads it closely and agrees with it. The paper reads like a considered judgment. Suppose {a_second}, who made the call first, hands in the very same paper. *The Irreducible Officer* calls the risk fluency substitution: polished analysis stands in for owned reasoning. Not every student who agrees with an AI fails this way. The task, the paper and all the answers are a constructed example.
page.editionNote: PME (professional military education): the original example from *The Irreducible Officer*, the National War College essay.
page.srTitle: Fluency substitution, an animated figure in ten beats
page.srSummary: An animated figure that opens on its name, Fluency substitution, failure mode 2 of 7, and builds a table. A red dot stands for a student with an example task: recommend whether to send forces to reassure a threatened ally. An AI drafts a polished paragraph, shown in grey on a beige band, the figure's mark for words the AI wrote: weigh escalation against the ally's trust; on balance, losing that trust is the greater risk, so the forces should go, with clear limits. The student reads it closely, strikes out one weak sentence and keeps the rest. A second student first writes their own call in a red note, "Send them. The ally's trust matters most, and troops show we mean it.", then has an AI draft from it. Suppose that draft matches the first paper word for word. Faculty receive two identical papers, both tagged as drafted with AI. With the papers set aside, they ask each student why, and both explain the call clearly; their answers appear in plain ink, as faculty hear them. Then faculty change one fact: what if the ally doesn't want our troops on its soil? The first student tries, and stays with the paper's call in its own words: on balance, losing that trust is still the greater risk, so the forces should go. The second says troops would now cost the ally's trust and proposes arms and aid instead. Only then do the answers take their colours: the first student's in the AI's grey, the second student's in red. The figure ends on the name and its definition, "Polished analysis stands in for owned reasoning.", then the faculty check and the follow-up: change one fact and ask what they would recommend now. Each beat is listed below with what is on screen.

page.checkFollow: Both students in the figure explain the call clearly without the paper. The second line separates them. Section VIII of the essay looks for the student who "revises under challenge rather than retreating to the artifact's language". In the oral defense in Section IX, {reviewer_ask_l} what evidence would change the recommendation.
page.quote: Fluency substitution is easier to miss. AI produces the tone of analytic maturity (balanced paragraphs, caveats in the right places, the measured voice of a considered judgment) and the student mistakes well-ordered language for well-owned reasoning. Researchers studying AI's effects on student cognition have introduced the concept of epistemic confinement to describe this condition: an illusion of competence while operating entirely within AI-constructed analytical boundaries, where the student believes they are thinking independently while the frame doing the work was never theirs ([Chow et al., 2026](https://ojs.aut.ac.nz/pjtel/article/view/246)). In strategy, fluency substitutes for deciding. A paragraph that balances every consideration may never identify which risk actually matters most.
page.cite: *The Irreducible Officer*, Section II, What the Problem Looks Like
